title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 26
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: An allotment association introduced a rule that plots left uncultivated for a season would be reallocated, and reports that the proportion of well-tended plots has risen. It concludes that the rule has made plot-holders more diligent.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The association has a waiting list of two years.
B. Some plot-holders objected to the rule.
C. Inspections are carried out in July.
D. Most of the improvement came from plots that changed hands under the rule, not from existing holders working harder.
E. The association charges an annual rent.
questions.explanation: Replacement rather than behaviour change produced the result, so the conclusion about diligence does not follow — though the rule worked in its own terms.

questions.prompt: A tyre recycling firm reports that the proportion of collected tyres it converts into rubber crumb rather than sending for incineration has risen from 40 to 70 per cent. It describes this as a substantial environmental improvement.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the description?
options: A. How much the crumb sells for
B. Whether the firm operates in more than one region
C. How many staff the firm employs
D. Whether incineration is regulated
E. Whether the total number of tyres collected changed over the same period
questions.explanation: A rising proportion of a growing total can leave more tyres incinerated than before, so the absolute figures are needed to assess the claim.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy introduced barcode scanning at the point of dispensing and reports that recorded dispensing errors fell by half. Managers conclude that scanning has halved dispensing errors.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Errors caught by the scanner and corrected before dispensing are now logged in a separate system and excluded from the recorded figure.
B. Scanning adds a few seconds to each dispensing.
C. Pharmacy staff received training on the system.
D. The pharmacy dispenses several thousand items a week.
E. Some medicines have no barcode.
questions.explanation: Reclassification removes errors from the measure without preventing them, so the recorded halving may reflect the accounting rather than the outcome.

questions.prompt: A sports injury clinic reports that patients who complete its full course of physiotherapy return to sport sooner than those who stop early, and urges all patients to complete the course.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the clinic's reasoning?
options: A. The full course costs more than a partial one.
B. Physiotherapists are qualified to the same standard.
C. Patients whose injuries respond quickly often stop attending once they feel recovered, while those with stubborn injuries continue to the end.
D. Some patients attend a clinic nearer their home.
E. The clinic treats amateur and professional athletes.
questions.explanation: If early stopping marks a good recovery, the association runs backwards — and in that case completing the course would not be what shortened the return.

questions.prompt: Every taxi permitted to use the Brancaster station rank is fitted with a card reader. No vehicle fitted with a card reader has received a complaint about refusing a short fare this year. Some taxis in the town have received such complaints.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Card readers prevent refusals.
B. Some taxis in the town are not permitted to use the station rank.
C. Most taxis have card readers.
D. No station rank taxi has ever refused a fare.
E. Complaints are made mainly about short journeys.
questions.explanation: Taxis with complaints have no card reader, and rank access requires one, so those taxis cannot use the rank. B claims a causal relation the statements do not establish.

questions.prompt: A podcast producer found that episodes released on Tuesdays are downloaded more often in their first week than episodes released on Fridays, and plans to release everything on Tuesdays.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the plan?
options: A. Downloads are counted automatically.
B. Some listeners subscribe to the feed.
C. Episodes remain available indefinitely.
D. The producer has always released its interviews with well-known guests on Tuesdays and its shorter episodes on Fridays.
E. The podcast is free to listeners.
questions.explanation: Release day is confounded with episode type, so moving the shorter episodes to Tuesday need not raise their downloads.

questions.prompt: A theatre reports that productions it markets with a discount preview week sell more tickets overall than productions without one, and concludes that preview discounts increase total sales.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Preview tickets are sold at half price.
B. Some audiences attend previews and return later.
C. The theatre offers preview weeks only for productions it expects to be popular, in order to build word of mouth.
D. The theatre seats four hundred people.
E. Productions run for three weeks on average.
questions.explanation: Selection by expected popularity means the discount marks the shows that would have sold well anyway.

questions.prompt: A launderette replaced its machines with larger-capacity ones and reports that its electricity use per kilogram of washing fell. The owner concludes that the new machines are more efficient.
questions.question: The conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Customers pay by the load rather than by weight.
B. Customers are not running the larger machines with partial loads more often than they ran the old ones full.
C. The machines were installed at the same time.
D. Electricity prices did not change.
E. The launderette is open the same hours as before.
questions.explanation: Consumption per kilogram depends on how full the drums run; the efficiency claim needs load behaviour not to have shifted the measure on its own.

questions.prompt: A housing association installed heat pumps in a hundred homes and reports that residents' heating bills fell by an average of 15 per cent. It concludes that heat pumps reduce heating costs.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Heat pumps require a hot water cylinder.
B. Some residents were unfamiliar with the controls.
C. The winter was of average severity.
D. Installation was funded by a grant.
E. The same homes were insulated during the installation programme, and homes insulated without a heat pump saw similar reductions.
questions.explanation: A comparison group receiving only the insulation attributes the saving to the insulation, and D removes the weather explanation rather than supplying one.

questions.prompt: A canal trust reports that stretches of towpath it has resurfaced carry more walkers than unresurfaced stretches, and argues that resurfacing the whole network would increase walking across the region.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the argument?
options: A. The trust resurfaced the stretches nearest towns first, where walker numbers were already highest.
B. Resurfacing is expensive.
C. Some walkers use the towpath to commute.
D. The network is two hundred miles long.
E. Unresurfaced stretches are muddy in winter.
questions.explanation: The resurfacing was allocated by existing use, so the comparison reflects location rather than surface.

questions.prompt: Supporters of closing a rural mobile library service argue that its costs per book borrowed are far higher than those of the town branch. Opponents reply that the service's users have no realistic alternative.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the opponents' reply?
options: A. The mobile library visits each village fortnightly.
B. The vehicle is due for replacement.
C. Book stock is shared with the town branch.
D. Most of its users are people who cannot drive and for whom the town branch is a two-hour round trip by an infrequent bus.
E. The service has operated for thirty years.
questions.explanation: It supplies the specific fact the reply depends on: the alternative is not available to the people using the service, which is what a cost-per-book comparison cannot see.

questions.passageText:
Rules requiring companies to disclose information assume that firms would otherwise say too little. Much of the time firms disclose more than the rules require, and understanding why illuminates what disclosure is for.

A firm with good news has an incentive to reveal it, since investors who cannot distinguish it from a mediocre firm will price it as average. Once the best firms disclose, the best of those remaining have the same incentive, and the argument iterates: silence becomes an admission, and a market can in principle unravel toward full disclosure without any rule at all.

Three things stop the unravelling. Disclosure can be costly in itself, revealing to competitors what a firm would rather they did not know, which is why research-intensive businesses disclose less about the same underlying facts. Some information cannot be verified, and an unverifiable claim conveys nothing because any firm could make it. And where a manager's own position depends on the news, the incentive to disclose promptly weakens exactly when the news is worst.

That last point explains the timing patterns that regulators watch. Bad news is disclosed disproportionately late on Fridays, before holidays, and bundled with other announcements. None of that is concealment in the legal sense, and all of it reduces the attention a disclosure receives. The regulatory response has been to specify not only what must be disclosed but when and how prominently — a shift from requiring information to requiring that it be findable, which is a different and harder thing to write into a rule.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, silence about a firm's results can become an admission because
options: A. regulators require an explanation for non-disclosure
B. investors assume that undisclosed information is fraudulent
C. once the best firms disclose, the best of those remaining have the same incentive
D. competitors publish comparable figures
E. auditors report on what was withheld
questions.explanation: The unravelling argument: each round of disclosure lowers what silence implies about those still silent.

questions.passageText:
Arranging the elements by atomic weight and grouping those with similar chemical behaviour produced, in the 1860s, an ordering that several people noticed. What distinguished Mendeleev's version was not the arrangement but what he was willing to do with it.

Where the sequence by weight conflicted with the grouping by behaviour, he trusted the behaviour and left gaps, asserting that undiscovered elements would fill them. He then specified what those elements would be like — atomic weight, density, the colour of the oxide, how the substance would behave with acids — in enough detail that the predictions could be wrong. When gallium, scandium and germanium were isolated and matched the descriptions closely, the arrangement stopped being a mnemonic and became a theory.

Two features of the episode are worth separating. The first is that a classification earns its status by making claims that could fail, and a scheme that accommodates whatever is discovered is doing less work than it appears to. The second is that the table was, at the time, unexplained. Nobody knew why elements should fall into periods; the underlying account, in terms of electron configuration, arrived half a century later.

That order matters for how the episode is usually taught. The table was not derived from atomic structure and then confirmed; it was an empirical regularity strong enough to predict before anyone could say why it held. A useful classification can precede its explanation, and demanding a mechanism before taking a pattern seriously would have delayed everything the table made possible.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, what distinguished Mendeleev's version of the table was
options: A. what he was willing to do with the arrangement
B. that he was the first to arrange elements by atomic weight
C. his access to newly isolated elements
D. his explanation of periodicity
E. the accuracy of the atomic weights he used
questions.explanation: The passage says several people noticed the ordering; the difference lay in trusting behaviour over weight and leaving gaps.

questions.passageText:
Clothing donated to charity in wealthy countries is sold in bulk, graded, and exported in quantity to markets in lower-income countries. The trade supports a great many jobs, supplies clothing cheaply, and has been blamed for the decline of domestic textile manufacturing in the countries that receive it. Each of those claims is partly right, and they are usually asserted rather than weighed.

The employment effect is real and rarely counted, because it is informal. Sorting, repairing, retailing and altering imported clothing occupies large numbers of traders and tailors, and a ban removes those livelihoods immediately while any manufacturing revival would be slow and uncertain.

The manufacturing claim is harder to establish than either side admits. Domestic textile industries in several receiving countries were already declining before second-hand imports became substantial, under pressure from cheap new clothing produced elsewhere and from the removal of protective tariffs. Studies attempting to isolate the effect of used-clothing imports find it real but smaller than the rhetoric implies, and dwarfed by competition from new low-cost imports.

The part of the trade that is unambiguously problematic is the residue. A substantial share of what is exported is unsellable on arrival and becomes waste in places with less capacity to handle it than the countries that discarded it. That is a transfer of disposal cost, it is measurable, and it is a stronger basis for regulating the trade than the manufacturing argument — but it points toward controlling what may be exported rather than banning the trade itself.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the employment supported by the second-hand clothing trade is rarely counted because it is
options: A. seasonal
B. informal
C. confined to exporting countries
D. concentrated in manufacturing
E. paid in kind
questions.explanation: Sorting, repairing, retailing and altering occupy traders and tailors outside formal statistics.

questions.passageText:
Ancient Greek and Latin were written without spaces between words and with almost no punctuation. Reading such a text is a skill, and the skill included working out where the units of sense fell — which is why reading aloud was normal, since the voice performed the parsing that the page did not supply.

Punctuation developed to serve that performance. The earliest systems marked places to breathe and where the pitch should rise or fall; the marks were rhetorical instructions rather than grammatical description. Word spacing spread later, in scribal centres where the copyists were not native speakers of Latin and could not rely on hearing the sense, and its arrival is associated with the growth of silent reading, which is faster because the eye can move ahead of any voice.

Printing then standardised what had been variable and personal. A compositor needed rules, and grammarians supplied them, which is how marks originally indicating how long to pause acquired the syntactic definitions taught today. The comma's modern job — separating clauses — is a description of what happens to fall where a reader once paused, and the two do not always coincide, which is the source of most disagreement about comma use.

Seen this way, the recurring complaint that punctuation is decaying looks different. The marks have changed function before, from breath to syntax, and are now under pressure from a written register that is closer to speech than anything printing dealt with. That is a change in what writing is being used for, and the historical record suggests punctuation follows use rather than restraining it.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the earliest punctuation marks were
options: A. grammatical descriptions of clause structure
B. introduced by printers
C. rhetorical instructions about breathing and pitch
D. used to separate words
E. confined to poetry
questions.explanation: The grammatical definitions came later, when printing required rules a compositor could apply.

The part of the trade that is unambiguously problematic is the residue. A substantial share of what is exported is unsellable on arrival and becomes waste in places with less capacity to handle it than the countries that discarded it. That is a transfer of disposal cost, it is measurable, and it is a stronger basis for regulating the trade than the manufacturing argument — but it points toward controlling what may be exported rather than banning the trade itself.

readingPassages.title: Marks on the Page
readingPassages.text:
Ancient Greek and Latin were written without spaces between words and with almost no punctuation. Reading such a text is a skill, and the skill included working out where the units of sense fell — which is why reading aloud was normal, since the voice performed the parsing that the page did not supply.

Punctuation developed to serve that performance. The earliest systems marked places to breathe and where the pitch should rise or fall; the marks were rhetorical instructions rather than grammatical description. Word spacing spread later, in scribal centres where the copyists were not native speakers of Latin and could not rely on hearing the sense, and its arrival is associated with the growth of silent reading, which is faster because the eye can move ahead of any voice.

Printing then standardised what had been variable and personal. A compositor needed rules, and grammarians supplied them, which is how marks originally indicating how long to pause acquired the syntactic definitions taught today. The comma's modern job — separating clauses — is a description of what happens to fall where a reader once paused, and the two do not always coincide, which is the source of most disagreement about comma use.

Seen this way, the recurring complaint that punctuation is decaying looks different. The marks have changed function before, from breath to syntax, and are now under pressure from a written register that is closer to speech than anything printing dealt with. That is a change in what writing is being used for, and the historical record suggests punctuation follows use rather than restraining it.
